3408    /// Both, and not just `Drop`, because the slot lives in a `moka` cache: `remove` hands the value
3409    /// back but drops the cache's own clone during a later maintenance pass, so a purely
3410    /// refcount-driven release would return the budget at an unpredictable time — and a node whose
3411    /// Sessions all closed could still refuse the next one. The explicit call makes the release
3412    /// simultaneous with the closure that caused it; the flag is what keeps the deferred drop from
3413    /// crediting it a second time.
3414    fn release(&self) {
3415        if self.released.swap(true, Ordering::Relaxed) {
3416            return;
3417        }
3418        // Saturating, so a release the flag somehow failed to suppress could not wrap the counter
3419        // into a budget that admits everything.
3420        let outstanding = self
3421            .outstanding
3422            .fetch_update(Ordering::Relaxed, Ordering::Relaxed, |held| {
3423                Some(held.saturating_sub(self.bytes))
3424            })
3425            .unwrap_or_default()
3426            .saturating_sub(self.bytes);
3427
3428        #[cfg(feature = "telemetry")]
3429        crate::telemetry::pix::record_cycle_bytes_released(self.bytes);
3430
3431        trace!(
3432            released = self.bytes,
3433            outstanding, "released live-cycle budget reservation"
3434        );
3435    }
3436}
3437
3438impl Drop for CycleBudgetReservation {
3439    fn drop(&mut self) {
3440        self.release();
3441    }
3442}
3443
3444/// Commits `guard`, admitting `session_id` into the SURB store for `capacity` SURBs.
3445///
3446/// Free function rather than a method on [`SessionManager`] because the guard borrows the manager's
3447/// cache, so a method would fight the same borrow the call sites are already inside. `surb_admission`
3448/// is passed separately for the same reason — the call sites hold `&self` while the guard holds the
3449/// cache borrow.
3450///
3451/// The slot is re-read from the cache rather than kept from allocation: the token `admit` returns has
3452/// to land in the *cached* copy of the slot, and that copy and the one the guard rolled in are two
3453/// clones of one value — see [`SessionSlot::claim_admission_token`] for why the cell they share is
3454/// behind an `Arc`. Re-reading is what keeps this honest when the cache has since handed the entry to
3455/// another reader: they all share the one cell.
3456///
3457/// An absent slot is not an error: the Session *was* established on this path, and `commit` runs with
3458/// `None` so the guard is still marked committed. The teardown that removed the slot already logged
3459/// "session closed", so skipping the commit here would leave that close unpaired (see
3460/// [`SessionSlotGuard::commit`]).
3461///
3462/// A slot found by key that is *not* the one this establishment allocated is treated exactly like an
3463/// absent one, and for the same reason: the re-read is by a reusable pseudonym, so between this
3464/// Session's `SessionEstablished` send and its parked commit a teardown can remove its slot and a
3465/// successor Session can be allocated under the same key. Admitting into the successor's slot would
3466/// stamp the successor's ring with this Session's token, and the successor's own commit would then
3467/// find the cell occupied and retire the successor's live admission — dropping a running Session to
3468/// the quarantine, the failure this whole seam exists to prevent. The guard holds its own slot's
3469/// [`AdmissionCell`], so the re-read can reject a foreign slot by identity; the commit itself still
3470/// runs, since this Session *was* established.
3471fn commit_slot_guard(
3472    guard: &mut SessionSlotGuard<'_>,
3473    sessions: &moka::sync::Cache<SessionId, SessionSlot>,
3474    session_id: SessionId,
3475    surb_admission: Arc<OnceLock<Arc<dyn SurbAdmissionControl>>>,
3476    capacity: usize,
3477) {
3478    // Re-read so the token lands in the cached copy; `None` means a teardown already removed it, and
3479    // the commit below still runs — only the admission is skipped. A slot that has since been
3480    // reallocated to another Session on this same pseudonym is discarded the same way: its cell is not
3481    // the guard's, so it is not this commit's to admit into.
3482    let slot = sessions
3483        .get(&session_id)
3484        .filter(|slot| Arc::ptr_eq(&slot.admission_token, guard.admission_token()));
3485
3486    guard.commit(
3487        slot.as_ref(),
3488        surb_admission.get().map(|a| a.as_ref() as &dyn SurbAdmissionControl),
3489        capacity,
3490    );
3491}
3492
3493/// RAII guard that rolls back a freshly inserted [`SessionSlot`] unless the
3494/// session setup is explicitly [committed](SessionSlotGuard::commit).
3495///
3496/// Establishing a session involves several fallible steps *after* the slot has
3497/// been inserted into the Session cache (constructing the [`HoprSession`],
3498/// notifying about the new session, sending the establishment message, ...).
3499/// If any of these steps fails, the already inserted slot would otherwise linger
3500/// in the cache until idle eviction, blocking the pseudonym (and counting towards
3501/// `maximum_sessions`) in the meantime.
3502///
3503/// Dropping this guard without committing removes the slot and tears down the
3504/// partially initialized session. Since Moka's removal is asynchronous and Rust
3505/// has no asynchronous `Drop`, the cleanup is performed on a spawned task.
3506struct SessionSlotGuard<'a> {
3507    sessions: &'a moka::sync::Cache<SessionId, SessionSlot>,
3508    active_sessions: Arc<std::sync::atomic::AtomicUsize>,
3509    session_id: SessionId,
3510    /// The SURB-store seam, cloned from the manager at allocation so `commit` and `Drop` can both
3511    /// reach it without holding the manager borrow. Held rather than looked up at call time because
3512    /// the rollback in `Drop` runs after the establishing task has already failed, and a guard that
3513    /// captured the manager's borrow there would fight the lifetimes for no gain.
3514    admission: Arc<OnceLock<Arc<dyn SurbAdmissionControl>>>,
3515    /// The packet pipeline's SURB-resolution window, cloned at allocation with the seam for the same
3516    /// reason: the rollback's deferred retire has to wait it out, and the guard outlives the
3517    /// establishing call that could otherwise read the manager's config.
3518    surb_resolution_wait: Duration,
3519    /// The admission-token cell of the slot this guard allocated, so a commit that re-reads the cache
3520    /// by key can tell its own slot from a successor's — see [`AdmissionCell`] and
3521    /// [`commit_slot_guard`].
3522    admission_cell: AdmissionCell,
3523    /// The instance of the slot this guard allocated; `commit` marks it established.
3524    instance: Arc<SlotInstance>,
3525    committed: bool,
3526}
3527
3528impl<'a> SessionSlotGuard<'a> {
3529    fn new(
3530        sessions: &'a moka::sync::Cache<SessionId, SessionSlot>,
3531        session_id: SessionId,
3532        active_sessions: Arc<std::sync::atomic::AtomicUsize>,
3533        admission: Arc<OnceLock<Arc<dyn SurbAdmissionControl>>>,
3534        surb_resolution_wait: Duration,
3535        admission_cell: AdmissionCell,
3536        instance: Arc<SlotInstance>,
3537    ) -> Self {
3538        Self {
3539            sessions,
3540            active_sessions,
3541            session_id,
3542            admission,
3543            surb_resolution_wait,
3544            admission_cell,
3545            instance,
3546            committed: false,
3547        }
3548    }
3549
3550    /// The admission-token cell of the slot this guard allocated. [`commit_slot_guard`] compares it
3551    /// against the cell of the slot the cache hands back for the same key, so a slot reallocated to a
3552    /// successor Session is recognised as foreign.
3553    fn admission_token(&self) -> &AdmissionCell {
3554        &self.admission_cell
3555    }
3556
3557    /// Marks the session as successfully established, preventing the slot from
3558    /// being rolled back when this guard is dropped.
3559    ///
3560    /// Logs "new session established" here, on both the Entry and the Exit side, so that every
3561    /// "session closed" line from [`close_session`] has a matching start line.
3562    ///
3563    /// This is also where the Session's pseudonym is admitted into the SURB store: deliberately
3564    /// here, at the point the Session becomes live, and not in
3565    /// [`allocate_session_slot`](SessionManager::allocate_session_slot), which runs while the Start
3566    /// handshake is still in flight — admitting there would put an unauthenticated peer into the
3567    /// store's admitted class, the exact state the admission control exists to prevent
3568    /// (hoprnet#8515). The Exit's negotiated ring target is likewise only known by the time its
3569    /// branch reaches `commit`, which allocation is too early to see.
3570    ///
3571    /// `admission` is `Some` on every production path — the guard carries the manager's seam, and
3572    /// `capacity` is the buffer target the ring is sized from. On the Exit that is the one the Entry
3573    /// announced, or the node's maximum when it announced none; the Entry's own commits always pass
3574    /// the node's `maximum_surb_buffer_size`. The `Option` keeps the guard usable from tests and
3575    /// callers that run without a store.
3576    ///
3577    /// The token `admit` returns lands in the slot's own cell rather than on the guard: the guard is
3578    /// gone by the time the Session is torn down, and the teardown reads the token from the slot it
3579    /// removes. Writing it here, after the `admit`, is what lets a later `release_session_slot`
3580    /// retire exactly this admission.
3581    ///
3582    /// `slot` is the cached copy when the caller could still find it *and* it is this establishment's
3583    /// own, and `None` when the slot was already torn down or has been reallocated to a successor
3584    /// Session on the same pseudonym — [`commit_slot_guard`] discards the latter before calling here.
3585    /// Committing without a slot is still a commit: the Session *was* established (the Exit sends
3586    /// `SessionEstablished` before it commits, so an Entry can close or answer with a
3587    /// `SessionId`-scoped `SessionError` in that window), so the guard must be marked committed, or
3588    /// `close_session` would log a "session closed" with no matching "new session established". Only
3589    /// the `admit` is skipped — there is no cell left to carry its token.
3590    ///
3591    /// When a slot *is* present, it is this Session's own (the caller checked), so its cell arbitrates
3592    /// against a teardown racing this commit and nothing else can be writing to it. The teardown claims
3593    /// the cell (see [`SessionSlot::claim_admission_token`]), so if this commit's own `set` fails, a
3594    /// teardown has already passed the point where it read the cell: it saw nothing to retire, and this
3595    /// admission would otherwise leak a ring no teardown ever removes. The commit therefore retires it
3596    /// — immediately, not deferred: the deferral exists so a closing Session's own return-routed
3597    /// notification still finds its ring, but here the Session is already gone and no packet of its is
3598    /// in flight for this admission, which was never visible to the pipeline.
3599    fn commit(&mut self, slot: Option<&SessionSlot>, admission: Option<&dyn SurbAdmissionControl>, capacity: usize) {
3600        self.committed = true;
3601        self.instance.mark_established();
3602        tracing::info!(session_id = %self.session_id, "new session established");
3603
3604        // Only a slot that is this Session's own can carry the admission's token to a teardown, so
3605        // `None` means nothing to admit for: either the Session was torn down — its teardown already
3606        // ran its (no-op) retire, and any batch a peer sends meanwhile lands in the quarantine like any
3607        // other unadmitted one — or the pseudonym was reallocated to a successor, whose ring is not
3608        // this admission's to stamp. The commit itself — the logging above — still happens.
3609        if let (Some(admission), Some(slot)) = (admission, slot) {
3610            // The Exit commits after it has answered `SessionEstablished`, so a `BalancerTarget`
3611            // keep-alive can have announced a raised target before the ring exists. Admit at the
3612            // larger of the two: the ring is sized once here, and a raise that arrived in that
3613            // window must not be lost until the Entry announces it again.
3614            let announced = capacity.max(slot.peek_raised_surb_target().unwrap_or(0));
3615            let token = admission.admit(&self.session_id, announced);
3616            if slot.admission_token.set(token).is_err() {
3617                // A teardown claimed the cell first, so nothing will retire this admission. Retire
3618                // it here — see the doc comment for why this is immediate rather than deferred.
3619                tracing::debug!(
3620                    session_id = %self.session_id,
3621                    "session was torn down while it committed; retiring the admission it could not record"
3622                );
3623                admission.retire(&self.session_id, token);
3624            } else if {
3625                // Pairs with the fence in `note_raised_surb_target`: either this side sees the
3626                // recorded target, or a concurrent keep-alive sees the token this `set` just wrote
3627                // and raises the ring itself. See that method for the failure the pair rules out.
3628                std::sync::atomic::fence(std::sync::atomic::Ordering::SeqCst);
3629                true
3630            } && let Some(raised) = slot.peek_raised_surb_target().filter(|&raised| raised > announced)
3631            {
3632                // The target moved again between the admit and the token being recorded; widen for
3633                // it rather than leave the ring a step behind until the next announcement.
3634                admission.raise_target(&self.session_id, token, raised);
3635            }
3636        }
3637    }
3638}
3639
3640impl Drop for SessionSlotGuard<'_> {
3641    fn drop(&mut self) {
3642        if !self.committed {
3643            // The session setup failed after the slot was inserted: remove it so it does
3644            // not block the pseudonym until idle eviction.
3645            let session_id = self.session_id;
3646            warn!(%session_id, "rolling back partially established session slot after setup failure");
3647            // Only this guard's own slot: the key is a reusable pseudonym, and the slot found there
3648            // may by now be a successor's. Matched by the admission cell, the guard's identity for it.
3649            let cell = &self.admission_cell;
3650            if let Some(slot) = remove_slot_if(self.sessions, &session_id, |slot| {
3651                Arc::ptr_eq(&slot.admission_token, cell)
3652            }) {
3653                self.active_sessions.fetch_sub(1, Ordering::Relaxed);
3654                // Not `close_session`: the Session was never established, so there is no
3655                // "session closed" line to pair with "new session established".
3656                //
3657                // The token is `NONE` by construction — admission happens at `commit`, and this
3658                // guard never committed — so the retire is the no-op that keeps every teardown wired
3659                // through the same seam without asking the store's accounting to trust that. Claiming
3660                // the cell rather than reading it keeps every teardown using one protocol.
3661                let token = slot.claim_admission_token();
3662                release_session_slot(
3663                    session_id,
3664                    slot,
3665                    ClosureReason::Eviction,
3666                    self.admission.get().cloned(),
3667                    surb_retire_grace(self.surb_resolution_wait),
3668                    token,
3669                );
3670            }
3671        }
3672    }
3673}
3674
3675/// Why an inbound packet was dropped without being delivered.
3676///
3677/// All of these are ordinary consequences of a session tearing down, of transient backpressure, or
3678/// of a peer sending traffic that is undecodable or names no local state. Reported as a
3679/// [`DispatchResult::Dropped`] outcome rather than an `Err` so the caller logs them quietly instead
3680/// of at `ERROR`.
3681#[derive(Clone, Copy, Debug, PartialEq, Eq)]
3682pub enum DropReason {
3683    /// The slot is still registered but its data sink (receiver) has been dropped
3684    /// (`TrySendError::Disconnected`). The common case when a session is being torn down.
3685    SinkClosed,
3686    /// The slot's inbox is full (`TrySendError::Full`): genuine backpressure, the reader is not
3687    /// keeping up. Distinct from [`SinkClosed`](Self::SinkClosed) because it is transient, not a
3688    /// teardown.
3689    SinkFull,
3690    /// No slot for this session id is registered (formerly the `UnknownData` error): the session
3691    /// was fully deregistered before this packet arrived.
3692    Unregistered,
3693    /// A Start-protocol message that names no state on this node it could ever be handled by:
3694    /// neither a Session slot nor a pending initiation under the pseudonym it arrives under. That
3695    /// includes one naming a *registered* Session under a mismatched sender pseudonym, which speaks
3696    /// about someone else's Session. Rejected at dispatch, before it can occupy a shared handler;
3697    /// benign, and quiet for the same reason the others are.
3698    StaleStartMessage,
3699    /// A Start-tagged packet that failed to decode. Anyone can send these for free, so the volume
3700    /// must never become the log.
3701    MalformedStartMessage,
3702    /// The bounded Start-protocol processing lane was full (`TrySendError::Full`): backpressure,
3703    /// not a teardown.
3704    StartQueueFull,
3705}
3706
3707/// Indicates the result of processing a message.
3708#[derive(Clone, Debug, PartialEq, Eq)]
3709pub enum DispatchResult {
3710    /// Session or Start protocol message has been processed successfully.
3711    Processed,
3712    /// The message was not related to Start or Session protocol.
3713    Unrelated(ApplicationDataIn),
3714    /// The message belonged to a session but could not be delivered and was dropped. Benign — see
3715    /// [`DropReason`]. Reported as `Ok` so the caller logs it quietly instead of as an `ERROR`.
3716    Dropped(DropReason),
3717}
3718
3719/// Configuration of the PIX protocol for incoming Sessions on Exit nodes.
3720#[derive(Clone, Debug, PartialEq, smart_default::SmartDefault, serde::Serialize, serde::Deserialize)]
3721#[serde(default, deny_unknown_fields)]
3722pub struct IncomingSessionPixConfig {
3723    /// If set to true, incoming Session without the [`Capability::UsePIX`] will be rejected.
3724    ///
3725    /// Default `false`.
3726    #[default(false)]
3727    pub enforce_pix: bool,
3728    /// Acceptable range of data quota in bytes.
3729    ///
3730    /// With dynamic SSA batches enabled, the Exit selects the smallest batch up to
3731    /// [`SupervisorConfig::ssas_per_request`] whose total `batch_size × quota_per_ssa` is inside this
3732    /// range. With dynamic batches disabled, the Entry's per-SSA quota itself must be inside the
3733    /// range and the configured batch size is used exactly. An offer that satisfies neither rule is
3734    /// rejected before the Session is established.
3735    ///
3736    /// The default is derived from the default PIX dimensions
3737    /// ([`crate::DEFAULT_PIX_POLYS_PER_SSA`] × ([`crate::DEFAULT_PIX_SHARES_PER_POLY`] +
3738    /// [`crate::DEFAULT_PIX_SURPLUS_SHARES`])) rather than hard-coded, so that an Entry running the
3739    /// default configuration is always accepted. The upper bound is exactly
3740    /// [`DEFAULT_PIX_SSA_QUOTA`]. Since every dynamic batch has at least one member, that upper bound
3741    /// still caps the data served by any one SSA cycle. Accepting larger dimensions would raise both
3742    /// that exposure and the reconstructor memory held per Session, so an Exit that wants to serve
3743    /// them must widen this range explicitly.
3744    ///
3745    /// The quota it is compared against counts the surplus — `polys × (threshold + surplus) ×
3746    /// PIX_QUOTA_BYTES_PER_SHARE` — so this bounds the traffic actually served rather than the
3747    /// fraction of it the threshold accounts for. It used to bound only the latter, which understated
3748    /// the exposure by the surplus factor: 3.47× at the deployed dimensions.
3749    ///
3750    /// Defaults to `DEFAULT_PIX_SSA_QUOTA / 4 ..= DEFAULT_PIX_SSA_QUOTA`
3751    /// (≈ 157 MiB to ≈ 630 MiB, inclusive).
3752    #[default(_code = "DEFAULT_PIX_SSA_QUOTA / DEFAULT_PIX_QUOTA_RANGE_SPAN..=DEFAULT_PIX_SSA_QUOTA")]
3753    pub quota_range: std::ops::RangeInclusive<u64>,
3754    /// Ceiling on the live Exit-side reconstructor state this node will commit to, in bytes.
3755    ///
3756    /// **This, not [`SessionManagerConfig::maximum_sessions`], is what bounds reconstructor
3757    /// memory.** A PIX Session reserves `MAX_OVERLAPPING_BATCHES × ssas_per_request ×
3758    /// hopr_protocol_pix::peak_cycle_bytes(offered params)` when it is accepted and holds it until
3759    /// it closes; a Session that does not fit is refused with
3760    /// [`StartErrorReason::NoSlotsAvailable`] before any state is allocated for it. The reservation
3761    /// is computed from the parameters the *peer* offered, so a Session asking for smaller
3762    /// dimensions costs proportionally less of the budget.
3763    ///
3764    /// Enforced at admission rather than validated as a product of the configuration, for the reason
3765    /// `SsaReconstructorConfig::max_ack_buffer_bytes` gives: `maximum_sessions` validates to
3766    /// 100 000, and the resulting product is a number no node could hold, so validating it would
3767    /// only ever reject the shipping defaults. Counting what has actually been committed to is
3768    /// indifferent to how the ceiling was configured.
3769    ///
3770    /// Default is 3 GiB. At the default dimensions a Session reserves ≈30.7 MiB — two overlapping
3771    /// batches of one cycle's peak each — so this admits 100 concurrent PIX Sessions with ≈1.7 MiB to
3772    /// spare, comfortably covering the 10–30 clients per Exit the calibration profile models. That
3773    /// is exactly the 100 Sessions a node manages by default (`maximum_managed_sessions`), which at
3774    /// these dimensions reserve ≈2.998 GiB — so with every default in place the two limits meet and
3775    /// this budget is what binds as soon as peers offer a costlier split of the same quota or that
3776    /// limit is raised. The margin is pinned by
3777    /// `default_live_cycle_budget_admits_the_default_managed_session_count`.
3778    ///
3779    /// A ceiling on *reservations*, not an allocation: nothing is claimed up front, and because the
3780    /// reservation is denominated at the adversarial peak, a node serving conforming peers holds an
3781    /// order of magnitude less than it has reserved. The number exists to stop an Exit selling more
3782    /// service than its memory can hold, not to describe what it will typically use.
3783    #[default(3 * 1024 * 1024 * 1024)]
3784    pub max_live_cycle_bytes: u64,
3785    /// Deadlines, fault limits and service budget the Exit-side PIX supervisor enforces on a
3786    /// Session.
3787    ///
3788    /// These live together rather than spread across this struct because they are only meaningful
3789    /// as a set: [`crate::validate_pix_supervision`] checks them against each other and against the
3790    /// reconstructor's lifetimes, and the node's config validator runs that at load time.
3791    pub supervision: SupervisorConfig,
3792    /// How long a paid PIX Session is kept after its data plane ends, awaiting its client's return.
3793    ///
3794    /// A client that reconnects under its paid pseudonym (see
3795    /// [`SessionClientConfig::pseudonym`](crate::SessionClientConfig::pseudonym)) would otherwise be
3796    /// refused for as long as the old slot lives, and would then pay a second deposit for a quota it
3797    /// has not used up. When the data plane of an Exit-side PIX Session ends because the client closed
3798    /// or dropped it (`EmptyRead`), and a cycle of the Session is paid for or the
3799    /// Entry has answered the commitment request, the Session is *detached* instead of drained or
3800    /// closed: the data path is cut, but the control plane (supervisor, egress gate, deposit
3801    /// observers, SURB ring, keep-alive and PIX fill) stays up for this long. An eligible
3802    /// re-initiation with the same pseudonym, PIX parameters, batch size and capabilities within the
3803    /// window takes it over and carries on the funded cycle. Without one, the window's expiry runs the
3804    /// ordinary drain-or-close path.
3805    ///
3806    /// The fill keeps running while detached, spending SURBs into the funded cycle at the rate the
3807    /// supervisor plans, so the Exit keeps recovering it through the gap, at the cost of some of the
3808    /// client's quota (about 0.5 to 3 % of a cycle over 60 s at the shipping dimensions).
3809    ///
3810    /// An operator close, a peer `SessionError` and every PIX failure skip the window.
3811    ///
3812    /// `0` disables detaching, and takeover altogether: a live Session is not taken over either.
3813    ///
3814    /// Capped by the session manager at half the session `idle_timeout` (one warning at construction
3815    /// when it applies), because the idle eviction would otherwise end the wait before the window
3816    /// did. A node with a short idle timeout therefore works with a shorter window, and is not
3817    /// refused its configuration.
3818    ///
3819    /// Only the client ending the stream (`EmptyRead`) starts a detach; the Exit's own application
3820    /// closing its end (`WriteClosed`) does not. Only a frame-based Session on the stateless socket
3821    /// (`Capability::Segmentation`, no retransmission) is ever detached or taken over, and only by an
3822    /// Entry that announces `Capability::Resumable`.
3823    ///
3824    /// The pseudonym alone authorises a takeover; see hoprnet#8723 for binding it to a secret of the
3825    /// original Entry.
3826    ///
3827    /// Default 60 s.
3828    #[default(Duration::from_secs(60))]
3829    #[serde(with = "humantime_serde")]
3830    pub resume_window: Duration,
3831}
3832
3833impl IncomingSessionPixConfig {
3834    /// The terms one Session is judged on, once the session server has had its say.
3835    ///
3836    /// The configured [`quota_range`](Self::quota_range) is an envelope, not a default: it is what
3837    /// [`validate_incoming_session_pix_config`] checked the deadlines and memory ceiling against,
3838    /// and what [`start_control_channel_capacity`] sized a preallocated ring from, both once at
3839    /// startup. So a decision's range is *intersected* with it rather than replacing it — a Session
3840    /// may be held to less than the node advertises, never to more than it was configured to
3841    /// honour. An operator wanting a wider class configures a wider envelope and narrows the rest.
3842    ///
3843    /// [`enforce_pix`](Self::enforce_pix) carries no such coupling and is simply overridden.
3844    fn effective_for(&self, decision: &SessionAdmissionDecision) -> EffectivePixAdmission {
3845        let quota_range = match &decision.pix_quota_range {
3846            Some(narrowed) => {
3847                *self.quota_range.start().max(narrowed.start())..=*self.quota_range.end().min(narrowed.end())
3848            }
3849            None => self.quota_range.clone(),
3850        };
3851
3852        EffectivePixAdmission {
3853            enforce_pix: decision.enforce_pix.unwrap_or(self.enforce_pix),
3854            quota_range,
3855            allow_dynamic_ssa_batches: self.supervision.allow_dynamic_ssa_batches,
3856            ssas_per_request: self.supervision.ssas_per_request,
3857        }
3858    }
3859
3860    /// The supervisor configuration for Sessions accepted under these settings.
3861    pub fn supervisor_config(&self) -> SupervisorConfig {
3862        self.supervision.clone()
3863    }
3864}
3865
3866/// The PIX terms a single incoming Session is admitted on.
3867///
3868/// Lighter than the whole [`IncomingSessionPixConfig`] because only these four fields vary per
3869/// Session: everything else the supervisor enforces is validated as a set at startup and stays
3870/// node-wide. Narrowing the quota only makes those deadlines more generous, which is why they need
3871/// not travel with it.
3872#[derive(Clone, Debug, PartialEq)]
3873pub(crate) struct EffectivePixAdmission {
3874    /// Whether this Session must offer PIX at all.
3875    enforce_pix: bool,
3876    /// Quota window this Session's offer must land in, already intersected with the node's envelope.
3877    quota_range: std::ops::RangeInclusive<SsaQuota>,
3878    /// Whether a batch may be derived from the offer, rather than taken as configured.
3879    allow_dynamic_ssa_batches: bool,
3880    /// Largest batch the Exit will ask for.
3881    ssas_per_request: usize,
3882}
3883
3884impl EffectivePixAdmission {
3885    /// Selects the batch size with which an Entry's per-SSA quota is acceptable.
3886    ///
3887    /// Dynamic mode walks from one upwards so it asks for no more Entry work, deposits or Exit
3888    /// reconstructor state than necessary. Fixed mode is the legacy rule: validate one SSA against
3889    /// the range, then request exactly the configured batch size.
3890    fn ssa_batch_size_for_quota(&self, quota_per_ssa: SsaQuota) -> Option<usize> {
3891        let configured_batch = self.ssas_per_request.clamp(1, MAX_SSA_BATCH_SIZE);
3892
3893        if !self.allow_dynamic_ssa_batches {
3894            return self.quota_range.contains(&quota_per_ssa).then_some(configured_batch);
3895        }
3896
3897        (1..=configured_batch).find(|batch_size| {
3898            quota_per_ssa
3899                .checked_mul(*batch_size as u64)
3900                .is_some_and(|batch_quota| self.quota_range.contains(&batch_quota))
3901        })
3902    }
3903}
3904
3905/// Bit position of the 64-bit options word within `StartInitiation::additional_data`.
3906///
3907/// The layout is: the low 32 bits carry the Entry's idle timeout (see [`into_initiation_additional_data`]),
3908/// bit 32 asks for forward receipts ([`FORWARD_RECEIPTS_REQUESTED`]), bit 33 marks a resume attempt
3909/// ([`INITIATION_RESUME_ATTEMPT`]), bits 34 to 63 are reserved for the resume secret (hoprnet#8723), and the
3910/// high 64 bits are the options word.
3911const INITIATION_OPTIONS_SHIFT: u32 = u64::BITS;
3912
3913/// Set in `StartInitiation::additional_data` by an Entry that wants forward receipts.
3914///
3915/// An Exit that predates it ignores the bit.
3916const FORWARD_RECEIPTS_REQUESTED: u128 = 1 << 32;
3917
3918/// Bit of `StartInitiation::additional_data` marking an attempt to resume a Session the Entry still holds PIX
3919/// state for. It is set only by the session manager, and an Exit that predates it ignores it.
3920const INITIATION_RESUME_ATTEMPT: u128 = 1 << 33;
3921
3922/// The bits of `StartInitiation::additional_data` that change a Session's behaviour, and that a takeover must carry
3923/// unchanged: the forward receipts request.
3924const INITIATION_BEHAVIOUR_BITS: u128 = FORWARD_RECEIPTS_REQUESTED;
3925
3926/// Whether `additional_data` marks a resume attempt; see [`INITIATION_RESUME_ATTEMPT`].
3927#[inline]
3928pub(crate) const fn announced_resume_attempt(additional_data: u128) -> bool {
3929    additional_data & INITIATION_RESUME_ATTEMPT != 0
3930}
3931
3932/// Packs the 64-bit options word into the most significant half of `StartInitiation::additional_data`, and
3933/// the Entry's idle timeout into its lowest 32 bits. No bit between them is set.
3934///
3935/// The timeout is in whole seconds, at least 1 for a nonzero one, saturating at `u32::MAX`; `0` means it is
3936/// not announced. The Exit bounds its idle report backoff by it (see [`session_idle_notify_cap`]).
3937#[inline]
3938fn into_initiation_additional_data(options: u64, entry_idle_timeout: Duration) -> u128 {
3939    let idle_secs = if entry_idle_timeout.is_zero() {
3940        0
3941    } else {
3942        entry_idle_timeout.as_secs().clamp(1, u32::MAX as u64) as u32
3943    };
3944    ((options as u128) << INITIATION_OPTIONS_SHIFT) | idle_secs as u128
3945}
3946
3947/// Inverse of [`into_initiation_additional_data`] for the options word, ignoring the least significant half.
3948#[inline]
3949const fn initiation_options(additional_data: u128) -> u64 {
3950    (additional_data >> INITIATION_OPTIONS_SHIFT) as u64
3951}
3952
3953/// The idle timeout the Entry announced in `additional_data`, or `None` if it announced none.
3954#[inline]
3955fn announced_idle_timeout(additional_data: u128) -> Option<Duration> {
3956    match additional_data as u32 {
3957        0 => None,
3958        secs => Some(Duration::from_secs(secs as u64)),
3959    }
3960}
3961
3962/// The longest idle report period for one Exit Session.
3963///
3964/// `configured` is the node's cap, already clamped to the Exit's own idle timeout. On an idle Session the
3965/// reports refresh the *Entry's* slot, so an Entry that announced its idle timeout bounds it further, to a
3966/// quarter of that (see [`IDLE_NOTIFY_PERIODS_PER_IDLE_TIMEOUT`]). An Entry that announced none is assumed to
3967/// use the Exit's.
3968fn session_idle_notify_cap(configured: Option<Duration>, entry_idle_timeout: Option<Duration>) -> Option<Duration> {
3969    let entry_cap = entry_idle_timeout
3970        .map(|idle| (idle / IDLE_NOTIFY_PERIODS_PER_IDLE_TIMEOUT).max(MIN_SURB_BUFFER_NOTIFICATION_PERIOD));
3971    match (configured, entry_cap) {
3972        (Some(configured), Some(entry_cap)) => Some(configured.min(entry_cap)),
3973        (configured, _) => configured,
3974    }
3975}
3976
3977/// Decodes the incentivization the Entry offered, before anyone is asked what to do about it.
3978///
3979/// `Ok(None)` is a peer that offered none. `Err` is one whose offer this node cannot read or
3980/// cannot share a curve with, which is refused on its own — no policy could rescue it, and both
3981/// questions are cheaper than the round trip to the session server that follows.
3982///
3983/// Split out from `SessionManager::check_pix_params` so the session server can be
3984/// told what was offered: it decides the terms, and terms relative to an offer need the offer.
3985fn decode_pix_offer(
3986    req: &StartInitiation<SessionTarget, HoprSessionCapabilities>,
3987) -> Result<Option<PixParams>, StartErrorReason> {
3988    if !req.capabilities.0.contains(Capability::UsePIX) {
3989        return Ok(None);
3990    }
3991
3992    // Unpacking is what enforces the protocol ranges on the three dimensions, and what rejects a
3993    // suite identifier no curve claims — leaving only "a known curve, but not ours" below.
3994    let params = PixParams::try_from_additional_data(initiation_options(req.additional_data)).map_err(|error| {
3995        debug!(
3996            challenge = req.challenge,
3997            %error,
3998            "client offered PIX parameters outside the protocol ranges"
3999        );
4000        StartErrorReason::UnacceptablePixParams
4001    })?;
4002
4003    // The Exit decides the curve, and it decides it by refusing anything else: nothing here
4004    // is negotiated, because there is nothing to negotiate — the suite is fixed at build
4005    // time on both sides. Checked before the quota because it is the cheaper question and
4006    // because a suite mismatch makes the dimensions meaningless anyway, and checked at all
4007    // because every later PIX field is sized by it. Refusing here means the Exit's own
4008    // commitments, the first curve-sized bytes in the exchange, are never sent to a peer
4009    // that would read their boundaries in the wrong place.
4010    if params.suite() != LOCAL_PIX_SUITE {
4011        debug!(
4012            challenge = req.challenge,
4013            offered = %params.suite(),
4014            ours = %LOCAL_PIX_SUITE,
4015            "refusing a client offering a PIX curve suite this node was not built for"
4016        );
4017        return Err(StartErrorReason::UnacceptablePixParams);
4018    }
4019
4020    Ok(Some(params))
4021}
4022
4023/// Validates the incoming-PIX invariants that span quota, supervision and memory settings.
4024///
4025/// `max_session_packet_rate` is the fastest a Session is assumed to go. Without fill it bounds
4026/// `max_recovery_time` directly; with fill it caps the `fill.max_rate` the deadline may count on.
4027pub fn validate_incoming_session_pix_config(
4028    cfg: &IncomingSessionPixConfig,
4029    max_session_packet_rate: u64,
4030) -> errors::Result<()> {
4031    if cfg.quota_range.is_empty() {
4032        return Err(TransportSessionError::InvalidConfig(
4033            "PIX quota_range must be non-empty (start must not exceed end)".into(),
4034        ));
4035    }
4036    if max_session_packet_rate == 0 {
4037        return Err(TransportSessionError::InvalidConfig(
4038            "maximum assumed PIX Session packet rate must be non-zero".into(),
4039        ));
4040    }
4041    // Named here although `validate_pix_supervision` also refuses it, because that runs later on both
4042    // paths: with fill enabled a zero deadline would otherwise surface as an infinite fill rate.
4043    if cfg.supervision.max_recovery_time.is_zero() {
4044        return Err(TransportSessionError::InvalidConfig(
4045            "PIX max_recovery_time must be non-zero".into(),
4046        ));
4047    }
4048
4049    let worst_cycle_packets = *cfg.quota_range.end() / PIX_QUOTA_BYTES_PER_SHARE;
4050
4051    // `max_recovery_time` has to leave a cycle of the widest accepted quota time to complete, and what
4052    // completes it depends on fill. With fill enabled the Exit finishes an under-served cycle itself, so
4053    // the bound is the fill ceiling's own arithmetic below. Without it only application traffic does,
4054    // and the Exit has no rate of its own to reason from.
4055    if cfg.supervision.fill.enabled {
4056        // The fill ceiling has to clear the rate a cycle of the widest accepted quota actually needs,
4057        // or the mechanism that exists to complete idle cycles cannot complete the very ones it
4058        // admits. The arithmetic is the planner's own, taken at the moment fill starts: the whole
4059        // cycle remains, the aim point sits `finish_fraction` of the way through `max_recovery_time`,
4060        // and the loss margin is paid on top. `max_recovery_time` is the *configured* per-cycle budget
4061        // rather than a deadline observed at run time, so this is a property of the configuration and
4062        // can be decided here.
4063        //
4064        // The ceiling counts only up to `max_session_packet_rate`: fill faster than any Session is
4065        // assumed to carry cannot finish a cycle any sooner.
4066        let fill = &cfg.supervision.fill;
4067        // Before the arithmetic, not after it. `validate_pix_supervision` also range-checks these two,
4068        // but it runs later on both paths that reach here — `SessionManager::start` calls this first,
4069        // and in `HoprProtocolConfig` this is a field validator while that is a schema-level one. The
4070        // `mul_f64` below panics on a `NaN` or negative fraction, so an unchecked one aborts the node
4071        // at config load rather than being reported; a fraction above one silently lowers the floor.
4072        crate::supervision::validate_fill_fractions(fill)?;
4073
4074        let horizon = cfg.supervision.max_recovery_time.mul_f64(fill.finish_fraction);
4075        // Still guarded although both factors are non-zero: a nanosecond-scale deadline times a
4076        // fraction rounds to zero, and dividing by it would report an infinite requirement.
4077        let floor = if horizon.is_zero() {
4078            u64::MAX
4079        } else {
4080            (worst_cycle_packets as f64 * (1.0 + fill.loss_margin) / horizon.as_secs_f64()).ceil() as u64
4081        };
4082        if (fill.max_rate as u64).min(max_session_packet_rate) < floor {
4083            let remedy = if floor > max_session_packet_rate {
4084                "raise max_recovery_time"
4085            } else {
4086                "raise fill.max_rate or max_recovery_time"
4087            };
4088            return Err(TransportSessionError::InvalidConfig(format!(
4089                "PIX fill.max_rate is {} (counted up to {max_session_packet_rate} packets/s), but the largest \
4090                 accepted quota ({} bytes) is {worst_cycle_packets} packets and needs at least {floor} packets/s to \
4091                 finish inside {horizon:?} with a {} loss margin; {remedy}",
4092                fill.max_rate,
4093                cfg.quota_range.end(),
4094                fill.loss_margin,
4095            )));
4096        }
4097    } else {
4098        // Refused only if even a Session at the fastest assumed rate could not finish a cycle in time,
4099        // so this rejects a deadline that is impossible rather than one that is merely tight.
4100        let needed = Duration::from_secs(worst_cycle_packets.div_ceil(max_session_packet_rate));
4101        if cfg.supervision.max_recovery_time < needed {
4102            return Err(TransportSessionError::InvalidConfig(format!(
4103                "PIX max_recovery_time is {:?}, but with fill disabled the largest accepted quota ({} bytes) is \
4104                 {worst_cycle_packets} packets and needs at least {needed:?} even at {max_session_packet_rate} \
4105                 packets/s",
4106                cfg.supervision.max_recovery_time,
4107                cfg.quota_range.end(),
4108            )));
4109        }
4110    }
4111
4112    let widest = max_cycle_budget_for_quota(*cfg.quota_range.end(), cfg.supervision.ssas_per_request);
4113    if cfg.max_live_cycle_bytes < widest {
4114        return Err(TransportSessionError::InvalidConfig(format!(
4115            "PIX max_live_cycle_bytes is {}, but one Session offering the largest accepted quota ({} bytes) reserves \
4116             up to {widest} bytes of reconstructor state",
4117            cfg.max_live_cycle_bytes,
4118            cfg.quota_range.end(),
4119        )));
4120    }
4121
4122    Ok(())
4123}
4124
4125/// Configuration for the [`SessionManager`].
4126#[derive(Clone, Debug, PartialEq, smart_default::SmartDefault)]
4127pub struct SessionManagerConfig {
4128    /// The maximum chunk of data that can be written to the Session's input buffer.
4129    ///
4130    /// Clamped to the socket's supported frame size range, preserving boundaries within that range.
4131    ///
4132    /// Default is [`SESSION_MTU`], i.e. exactly one segment per frame.
4133    #[default(SESSION_MTU)]
4134    pub frame_mtu: usize,
4135
4136    /// The maximum time for an incomplete frame to stay in the Session's output buffer.
4137    ///
4138    /// Must exceed the worst-case SURB replenishment latency on the return path.
4139    /// The SURB balancer replenishes via KeepAlive every ~2 s; the retry loop in
4140    /// the routing resolver sleeps 5 ms per attempt and can block for the full
4141    /// replenishment cycle.  Setting this below the KeepAlive period causes the
4142    /// sequencer to discard frames that arrive after a SURB-starved peer finally
4143    /// gets new SURBs and sends its echo.
4144    ///
4145    /// Default is 3 s.
4146    #[default(Duration::from_secs(3))]
4147    pub max_frame_timeout: Duration,
4148
4149    /// Maximum number of segments to buffer in the downstream transport of a Session's socket.
4150    /// If 0 is given, the transport is unbuffered.
4151    ///
4152    /// Default is 0.
4153    #[default(0)]
4154    pub max_buffered_segments: usize,
4155
4156    /// Abandon the frame due next once this many later frames are waiting behind it, rather than
4157    /// holding them for the whole of [`Self::max_frame_timeout`].
4158    ///
4159    /// The two answer different questions. `max_frame_timeout` is how long a *missing* frame is
4160    /// waited for, and is set here to exceed the ~2 s SURB KeepAlive so a starved peer's late echo
4161    /// is not discarded. This bounds how much *already received* data is held hostage during that
4162    /// wait -- a cost paid once per gap, which compounds as later frames queue up.
4163    ///
4164    /// Without it, a session that cannot retransmit waits the full timeout for a frame that will
4165    /// never arrive. Measured on a 5-node cluster after killing a return relayer: 98.5 % of bytes
4166    /// returned over the wire, 0.60 % reached the application, and the application-side
4167    /// inter-arrival median sat exactly on the 3 s timeout.
4168    ///
4169    /// The right value tracks reordering depth -- throughput x latency spread / frame size -- so
4170    /// it is deployment-specific. Tune with `SessionConfig::max_frames_behind_gap`; too low converts
4171    /// ordinary reordering into loss, too high leaves the stall in place.
4172    ///
4173    /// Default is 256, which is roughly 3-4x the reordering depth of the cluster it was measured
4174    /// on (~0.5 MB/s over paths spread across 10-260 ms, 1500 B frames, so ~70-85 frames in
4175    /// flight out of order). The margin is not cosmetic: at 64 -- about one reordering depth --
4176    /// a *healthy* baseline dropped from 100 % to 92.2 % arrival, because ordinary reordering was
4177    /// being read as loss. At 256 the same baseline returned 100 % while a return relayer killed
4178    /// mid-session still recovered 97.1 %, against 0.60 % with the bound absent.
4179    ///
4180    /// Default is 256.
4181    #[default(Some(256))]
4182    pub max_frames_behind_gap: Option<usize>,
4183
4184    /// The base timeout for initiation of Session initiation.
4185    ///
4186    /// The actual timeout is adjusted according to the number of hops for that Session:
4187    /// `t = initiation_time_out_base * (num_forward_hops + num_return_hops + 2)`
4188    ///
4189    /// Default is 500 milliseconds.
4190    #[default(Duration::from_millis(500))]
4191    pub initiation_timeout_base: Duration,
4192
4193    /// The first gap before the Entry repeats an unanswered `StartSession`; each further gap doubles.
4194    ///
4195    /// A repeat is sent only before the initiation deadline, which does not move. Default is 1 second.
4196    #[default(Duration::from_secs(1))]
4197    pub initiation_resend_interval: Duration,
4198
4199    /// How many times the Entry repeats an unanswered `StartSession`.
4200    ///
4201    /// Default is 3; 0 sends the request once, as before.
4202    #[default(3)]
4203    pub max_initiation_resends: u32,
4204
4205    /// Timeout for Session to be closed due to inactivity.
4206    ///
4207    /// Default is 180 seconds.
4208    #[default(Duration::from_secs(180))]
4209    pub idle_timeout: Duration,
4210
4211    /// Minimum interval at which an establishing Session's cache slot is refreshed
4212    /// ("touched") to keep [`idle_timeout`](Self::idle_timeout) from evicting it while
4213    /// SURBs pre-load.
4214    ///
4215    /// The touch period is [`idle_timeout`](Self::idle_timeout)` / 2`, floored to this
4216    /// value so it never drops below a sane minimum for very short idle timeouts.
4217    ///
4218    /// Default is 100 milliseconds.
4219    #[default(Duration::from_millis(100))]
4220    pub min_session_touch_period: Duration,
4221
4222    /// The sampling interval for SURB balancer.
4223    /// It will make SURB control decisions regularly at this interval.
4224    ///
4225    /// Default is 100 milliseconds.
4226    #[default(Duration::from_millis(100))]
4227    pub balancer_sampling_interval: Duration,
4228
4229    /// Initial packets per second egress rate on an incoming Session.
4230    ///
4231    /// This only applies to incoming Sessions without the [`Capability::NoRateControl`] flag set.
4232    ///
4233    /// Default is 10 packets/second.
4234    #[default(10)]
4235    pub initial_return_session_egress_rate: usize,
4236
4237    /// Minimum period of time for which a SURB buffer at the Exit must
4238    /// endure if no SURBs are being received.
4239    ///
4240    /// In other words, it is the minimum period of time an Exit must withstand when
4241    /// no SURBs are received from the Entry at all. To do so, the egress traffic
4242    /// will be shaped accordingly to meet this requirement.
4243    ///
4244    /// This only applies to incoming Sessions without the [`Capability::NoRateControl`] flag set.
4245    ///
4246    /// Default is 5 seconds, minimum is 1 second.
4247    #[default(Duration::from_secs(5))]
4248    pub minimum_surb_buffer_duration: Duration,
4249
4250    /// Indicates the maximum number of SURBs in the SURB buffer to be requested when creating a new Session.
4251    ///
4252    /// This value is theoretically capped by the size of the global transport SURB ring buffer,
4253    /// so values greater than that do not make sense. This value should be ideally set equal
4254    /// to the size of the global transport SURB RB.
4255    ///
4256    /// On the Exit it is also the largest target it takes from an Entry, and the target the SURB ring of
4257    /// a Session is sized from when its Entry announces none.
4258    ///
4259    /// Default is 10 000 SURBs.
4260    #[default(10_000)]
4261    pub maximum_surb_buffer_size: usize,
4262
4263    /// If set, the Session recipient (Exit) will notify the Session initiator (Entry) about
4264    /// its SURB balance for the Session using keep-alive packets periodically.
4265    ///
4266    /// Keep in mind that each notification also costs 1 SURB, so the notification period should
4267    /// not be too frequent.
4268    ///
4269    /// The Exit sends it only to an Entry that has shown it runs a SURB balancer, by having sent a
4270    /// keep-alive (whether or not that keep-alive announces a target, but not a manual ping), and only while the
4271    /// Exit's own estimate of the SURBs it holds for the Session is above 0. An Entry without a balancer
4272    /// attaches a SURB to each data packet and reads no report. The notification carries the Exit
4273    /// balancer's level on a rate-controlled Session, and the Exit's own count of its SURBs on a
4274    /// `NoRateControl` one, which runs no balancer.
4275    ///
4276    /// Default is None (no notification sent to the client), minimum is 1 second.
4277    #[default(None)]
4278    pub surb_balance_notify_period: Option<Duration>,
4279
4280    /// The longest period the Exit's SURB-level report backs off to on an idle Session; see
4281    /// `PixFillControl::admit` for the rules.
4282    ///
4283    /// Floored at `MIN_SURB_BUFFER_NOTIFICATION_PERIOD` and clamped to `idle_timeout / 4`, because on an idle
4284    /// Session these reports refresh the Entry's slot timer. Per Session it is further bounded to a quarter of
4285    /// the idle timeout the Entry announces; an Entry that announces none is assumed to use this node's. `None`,
4286    /// or a value not above [`surb_balance_notify_period`](Self::surb_balance_notify_period), disables the
4287    /// backoff.
4288    ///
4289    /// Default is `None` here; the node's default is in the transport configuration.
4290    #[default(None)]
4291    pub surb_idle_notify_period: Option<Duration>,
4292
4293    /// The period the Exit reports its SURB level at while the Session's forward path is degraded.
4294    ///
4295    /// The Exit's level reports are the only replies that reach the Entry when the forward path goes
4296    /// dark — the data frames never reassemble, so no echo reply goes out. A report per
4297    /// [`surb_balance_notify_period`](Self::surb_balance_notify_period) (15 s by default) therefore
4298    /// leaves the Entry's verdict on a dead relayer waiting for the report, measured at +12 to +28 s
4299    /// after the kill instead of the ~+11 s an intact forward path gives.
4300    ///
4301    /// This is that period for the duration of the degradation: while the Session has lost a frame
4302    /// within the last three seconds, its Entry has shown it reads the reports, and its SURB stock is
4303    /// above the keep-alive reserve, the Exit reports this often instead. The cost is bounded by
4304    /// both the hold and the reserve: at most one SURB per report, never into the reserve, and the
4305    /// normal period resumes within three seconds and one poll of the last loss.
4306    ///
4307    /// `None` disables it. A value at or above [`surb_balance_notify_period`](Self::surb_balance_notify_period)
4308    /// is treated as disabled, since it would report no faster; so is a value on a Session with no
4309    /// notification period at all. Minimum is 1 second.
4310    #[default(Some(MIN_SURB_BUFFER_NOTIFICATION_PERIOD))]
4311    pub surb_degraded_notify_period: Option<Duration>,
4312
4313    /// If set, the Session initiator (Entry) will notify the Session recipient (Exit) about
4314    /// the local SURB balancer target using keep-alive packets from the SURB balancer.
4315    ///
4316    /// This is useful when the client plans to change the SURB balancer target dynamically.
4317    ///
4318    /// For a Session that announced a target, the Exit sizes the SURB ring from it, and widens the ring
4319    /// when a raised one arrives. A rate-controlled Exit also takes its balancer's set-point, its egress
4320    /// cap (`max_surbs_per_sec`) and the SURB reserve it holds back for its keep-alives from the target,
4321    /// and follows every change the Entry announces, lowered as well as raised.
4322    ///
4323    /// With this off, the Exit only knows the target announced at establishment, and no change to it
4324    /// is seen, lower or higher. A rate-controlled Exit then keeps its ring, balancer, egress cap and
4325    /// keep-alive reserve at the establishment target: an Entry that raises its target does not lift
4326    /// the Exit's egress cap or widen its ring, and one that lowers it to that reserve or below may
4327    /// leave the Exit holding its data back for good, waiting for a stock the Entry no longer keeps. A
4328    /// Session that announces no target at establishment, as an Entry without a SURB balancer or any
4329    /// `NoRateControl` Entry does, gets the full ring from the start, so turning this off costs it
4330    /// nothing. The Exit's SURB-level reports are unaffected: it recognises a balancing Entry by its
4331    /// balancer's keep-alives, flagged or not.
4332    ///
4333    /// Default is true.
4334    #[default(true)]
4335    pub surb_target_notify: bool,
4336
4337    /// Maximum number of concurrent sessions allowed.
4338    ///
4339    /// Default is 10_000.
4340    #[default(10_000)]
4341    pub maximum_sessions: usize,
4342
4343    /// How many packets can be buffered if the [`HoprSession`] input socket is not fast enough.
4344    ///
4345    /// Controls the capacity of the internal `crossfire` channel used for each session slot.
4346    ///
4347    /// Default is 10 000.
4348    #[default(10000)]
4349    pub session_forward_capacity: usize,
4350
4351    /// Configuration of the PIX protocol for the Exit nodes.
4352    pub pix_config: IncomingSessionPixConfig,
4353
4354    /// Maximum number of SSA commitments this node, acting as an Entry, will accept in a single
4355    /// [`SsaServerCommitmentMessage`].
4356    ///
4357    /// This is the Entry's protection against a misbehaving Exit, not a preference: every accepted
4358    /// entry costs a full `new_ssa_commitment`, thousands of outbound `SsaCommit` packets and its own
4359    /// on-chain deposit, so without a cap one inbound packet amplifies into minutes of CPU, a large
4360    /// packet burst, and as many simultaneous deposits as the wire format admits. An over-cap request
4361    /// is rejected in full, before any commitment is generated or any `ReadyToDeposit` is emitted, and
4362    /// the Exit is told with a `SessionError` — see `refuse_ssa_request`.
4363    ///
4364    /// It must be at least the `ssas_per_request` of every Exit this node connects to — see
4365    /// [`SupervisorConfig::ssas_per_request`](crate::SupervisorConfig::ssas_per_request) for why a mismatch
4366    /// loses every Session.
4367    ///
4368    /// Clamped to `1..=`[`MAX_SSA_BATCH_SIZE`] in [`SessionManager::new`].
4369    ///
4370    /// Defaults to [`DEFAULT_MAX_SSAS_PER_SSA_REQUEST`] (2).
4371    #[default(DEFAULT_MAX_SSAS_PER_SSA_REQUEST)]
4372    pub max_ssas_per_ssa_request: usize,
4373
4374    /// How long the Exit waits for the session server to say whether a Session is admitted.
4375    ///
4376    /// The wait sits inside the peer's own initiation timeout, so it has to be comfortably shorter
4377    /// than [`initiation_timeout_base`](Self::initiation_timeout_base): a server slower than the
4378    /// peer is patient refuses every Session it is asked about, and does so after the peer has
4379    /// already given up. [`SessionManager::new`] rejects a configuration where it is not.
4380    ///
4381    /// Expiring refuses the Session — the alternative, admitting on the node's own terms, would let
4382    /// an overloaded or wedged server silently disable every rule the operator wrote.
4383    ///
4384    /// Default is 2 seconds.
4385    #[default(Duration::from_secs(2))]
4386    pub session_admission_timeout: Duration,
4387
4388    /// How long the packet pipeline retries a return-routed packet whose SURBs have not arrived
4389    /// before dropping it.
4390    ///
4391    /// The composition root supplies this from its own packet-pipeline config, because the retire of
4392    /// a closing Session's SURB admission must wait it out — the teardown's grace is this window plus
4393    /// a small margin. A Session
4394    /// teardown that retired before the window closed would drop the closing Exit's own
4395    /// return-routed notification mid-lookup, and the Entry would then never learn that its Session
4396    /// was gone. The manager cannot see the pipeline config, so it is threaded here rather than
4397    /// pinned against a default that an operator's larger setting would silently invalidate.
4398    ///
4399    /// Default is 6 seconds, the packet pipeline's own default.
4400    #[default(Duration::from_secs(6))]
4401    pub surb_resolution_wait: Duration,
4402
4403    /// How many refusal replies the Exit sends to refused `StartSession`s, across all reasons; see
4404    /// [`RefusalReplyBudget`]. `None` answers every refusal.
4405    ///
4406    /// Default is [`RefusalReplyBudget::default`].
4407    #[default(Some(RefusalReplyBudget::default()))]
4408    pub refusal_reply_budget: Option<RefusalReplyBudget>,
4409
4410    /// Whether an Entry asks for forward receipts and an Exit sends them.
4411    ///
4412    /// Default is true.
4413    #[default(true)]
4414    pub forward_receipts: bool,
4415}

4417// Type-erased sink used by the `SessionManager` to notify about newly incoming sessions.
4418// The errors produced by the underlying sink are remapped into `SessionManagerError`.
4419type BoxSink<T> = Pin<Box<dyn Sink<T, Error = SessionManagerError> + Send>>;
4420
4421type SessionNotifiers = (
4422    Arc<hopr_utils::runtime::prelude::Mutex<BoxSink<IncomingSession>>>,
4423    crossfire::MTx<crossfire::mpsc::Array<(SessionId, ClosureReason, Arc<SlotInstance>)>>,
4424);

4426/// What an incoming packet did to the SURB store, as the packet pipeline reported it.
4427///
4428/// Carried to the Start protocol handler along with the message, because the conversion of the packet's
4429/// data into a [`HoprStartProtocol`] drops the packet info, and with it these two counts. Booked with
4430/// [`account_incoming_surbs`].
4431#[derive(Clone, Copy, Debug, Default, PartialEq, Eq)]
4432struct SurbsStored {
4433    /// SURBs the packet carried, clamped to what fits beside its message
4434    /// ([`ApplicationDataIn::num_surbs_with_msg`]).
4435    saved: u64,
4436    /// SURBs the store lost on arrival: dropped for capacity, and, since a newer SURB generation clears
4437    /// the store, the stock that generation wiped (`IncomingPacketInfo::num_evicted_surbs`).
4438    evicted: u64,
4439}
4440
4441impl SurbsStored {
4442    fn of(data: &ApplicationDataIn) -> Self {
4443        Self {
4444            saved: data.num_surbs_with_msg() as u64,
4445            evicted: data.packet_info.num_evicted_surbs as u64,
4446        }
4447    }
4448}

4450// Sink for processing Start protocol messages, each with what its packet did to the SURB store.
4451// Must be within Arc to be shared across SessionManager clones.
4452// The inner OnceLock is set once in `start()` and read in `dispatch_message`.
4453// The packet info travels along because a Start message cannot always be judged by its content alone:
4454// see `refuse_pix_over_direct_return_path`. What the packet did to the SURB store travels too, taken
4455// before the conversion into a `HoprStartProtocol` consumes the data it is counted from: the part
4456// dispatch could not book itself, which is all of it only for an opening that creates its Session.
4457type StartMessage = (
4458    HoprPseudonym,
4459    HoprStartProtocol,
4460    IncomingPacketInfo,
4461    SurbsStored,
4462    tracing::Span,
4463);
4464type StartProtocolMsgSink = Arc<OnceLock<crossfire::MTx<crossfire::mpsc::Array<StartMessage>>>>;

4466/// PIX protocol toolbox to enable [`SessionManager`] to use PIX protocol.
4467#[derive(Clone)]
4468pub struct PixToolbox {
4469    share_generator: Arc<SsaShareGenerator<HoprPixSpec>>,
4470    share_processor: Arc<SsaReconstructor<HoprPixSpec>>,
4471    pix_events: crossfire::MTx<crossfire::mpsc::Array<HoprSessionOutPixEvent>>,
4472}
4473
4474impl PixToolbox {
4475    pub fn new(
4476        share_generator: Arc<SsaShareGenerator<HoprPixSpec>>,
4477        share_processor: Arc<SsaReconstructor<HoprPixSpec>>,
4478    ) -> (Self, impl futures::Stream<Item = HoprSessionOutPixEvent>) {
4479        let (pix_events, pix_events_rx) = crossfire::mpsc::bounded_blocking_async::<HoprSessionOutPixEvent>(1024);
4480        (
4481            Self {
4482                share_generator,
4483                share_processor,
4484                pix_events,
4485            },
4486            pix_events_rx.into_stream(),
4487        )
4488    }
4489}

4491/// Manages lifecycles of Sessions.
4492///
4493/// Once the manager is [started](SessionManager::start), the [`SessionManager::dispatch_message`]
4494/// should be called for each [`ApplicationData`] received by the node.
4495/// This way, the `SessionManager` takes care of proper Start sub-protocol message processing
4496/// and correct dispatch of Session-related packets to individual existing Sessions.
4497///
4498/// Secondly, the manager can initiate new outgoing sessions via [`SessionManager::new_session`],
4499/// probe sessions using [`SessionManager::ping_session`]
4500/// and list them via [`SessionManager::active_sessions`].
4501///
4502/// Since the `SessionManager` operates over the HOPR protocol,
4503/// the message transport `S` is required.
4504/// Such transport must also be `Clone`, since it will be cloned into all the created [`HoprSession`] objects.
4505///
4506/// ## SURB balancing
4507///
4508/// The manager also can take care of automatic [SURB balancing](SurbBalancerConfig) per Session.
4509///
4510/// With each packet sent from the session initiator over to the receiving party, zero to 2 SURBs might be delivered.
4511/// When the receiving party wants to send reply packets back, it must consume 1 SURB per packet. This
4512/// means that if the difference between the SURBs delivered and SURBs consumed is negative, the receiving party
4513/// might soon run out of SURBs. If SURBs run out, the reply packets will be dropped, causing likely quality of
4514/// service degradation.
4515///
4516/// In an attempt to counter this effect, there are two co-existing automated modes of SURB balancing:
4517/// *local SURB balancing* and *remote SURB balancing*.
4518///
4519/// ### Local SURB balancing
4520///
4521/// Local SURB balancing is performed on the sessions that were initiated by another party (and are
4522/// therefore incoming to us).
4523/// The local SURB balancing mechanism continuously evaluates the rate of SURB consumption and retrieval,
4524/// and if SURBs are running out, the packet egress shaping takes effect. This by itself does not
4525/// avoid the depletion of SURBs but slows it down in the hope that the initiating party can deliver
4526/// more SURBs over time. This might happen either organically by sending effective payloads that
4527/// allow non-zero number of SURBs in the packet, or non-organically by delivering KeepAlive messages
4528/// via *remote SURB balancing*. Both are governed by the initiator's estimate of our buffer, so
4529/// signalling SURB distress is what tells it to keep the organic ones coming.
4530///
4531/// The egress shaping is done automatically, unless the Session initiator sets the [`Capability::NoRateControl`]
4532/// flag during Session initiation.
4533///
4534/// ### Remote SURB balancing
4535///
4536/// Remote SURB balancing is performed by the Session initiator. The SURB balancer estimates the number of SURBs
4537/// delivered to the other party, and also the number of SURBs consumed by seeing the amount of traffic received
4538/// in replies.
4539/// When enabled, a desired target level of SURBs at the Session counterparty is set. According to measured
4540/// inflow and outflow of SURBs to/from the counterparty, the production of non-organic SURBs is started
4541/// via keep-alive messages (sent to counterparty) and is controlled to maintain that target level.
4542///
4543/// In other words, the Session initiator tries to compensate for the usage of SURBs by the counterparty by
4544/// sending new ones via the keep-alive messages.
4545///
4546/// The same estimate also governs *organic* production: once the counterparty is estimated to be at
4547/// its target, outgoing Session data packets carry no SURBs at all, and they return to one per packet
4548/// as soon as the estimate falls back below target. Without that, a balancer could correctly silence
4549/// its keep-alives while organic SURBs kept pouring into a full buffer — where each one evicts an
4550/// older SURB and destroys the PIX share it was carrying. A `SurbDistress` or `OutOfSurbs` signal
4551/// from the counterparty overrides the estimate and restores production immediately, which is what
4552/// makes it safe to act on an estimate that forward-path loss can inflate.
4553///
4554/// This mechanism is configurable via the `surb_management` field in [`SessionClientConfig`].
4555///
4556/// ### Possible scenarios
4557///
4558/// There are 4 different scenarios of local vs. remote SURB balancing configuration, but
4559/// an equilibrium (= matching the SURB production and consumption) is most likely to be reached
4560/// only when both are configured (the ideal case below):
4561///
4562/// #### 1. Ideal local and remote SURB balancing
4563///
4564/// 1. The Session recipient (Exit) set the `initial_return_session_egress_rate`, `max_surb_buffer_duration` and
4565///    `maximum_surb_buffer_size` values in the [`SessionManagerConfig`].
4566/// 2. The Session initiator (Entry) sets the [`target_surb_buffer_size`](SurbBalancerConfig) which matches the
4567///    [`maximum_surb_buffer_size`](SessionManagerConfig) of the counterparty.
4568/// 3. The Session initiator (Entry) does *NOT* set the [`Capability::NoRateControl`] capability flag when opening
4569///    Session.
4570/// 4. The Session initiator (Entry) sets [`max_surbs_per_sec`](SurbBalancerConfig) slightly higher than the
4571///    `maximum_surb_buffer_size / max_surb_buffer_duration` value configured at the counterparty.
4572///
4573/// In this situation, the maximum Session egress from Exit to the Entry is given by the
4574/// `maximum_surb_buffer_size / max_surb_buffer_duration` ratio. If there is enough bandwidth,
4575/// the (remote) SURB balancer sending SURBs to the Exit will stabilize roughly at this rate of SURBs/sec,
4576/// and the whole system will be in equilibrium during the Session's lifetime (under ideal network conditions).
4577///
4578/// #### 2. Remote SURB balancing only
4579///
4580/// 1. The Session initiator (Entry) *DOES* set the [`Capability::NoRateControl`] capability flag when opening Session.
4581/// 2. The Session initiator (Entry) sets `max_surbs_per_sec` and `target_surb_buffer_size` values in
4582///    [`SurbBalancerConfig`]
4583///
4584/// In this one-sided situation, the Entry node floods the Exit node with SURBs,
4585/// only based on its estimated consumption of SURBs at the Exit. The Exit's egress is not
4586/// rate-limited at all. If the Exit runs out of SURBs at any point in time, it will simply drop egress packets.
4587///
4588/// This configuration could potentially only lead to an equilibrium
4589/// when the `SurbBalancer` at the Entry can react fast enough to Exit's demand.
4590///
4591/// #### 3. Local SURB balancing only
4592///
4593/// 1. The Session recipient (Exit) set the `initial_return_session_egress_rate`, `max_surb_buffer_duration` and
4594///    `maximum_surb_buffer_size` values in the [`SessionManagerConfig`].
4595/// 2. The Session initiator (Entry) does *NOT* set the [`Capability::NoRateControl`] capability flag when opening
4596///    Session.
4597/// 3. The Session initiator (Entry) does *NOT* set the [`SurbBalancerConfig`] at all when opening Session.
4598///
4599/// In this one-sided situation, the Entry node does not provide any additional SURBs at all (except the
4600/// ones that are naturally carried by the egress packets which have space to hold SURBs). It relies
4601/// only on the Session egress limiting of the Exit node.
4602/// The Exit will limit the egress roughly to the rate of natural SURB occurrence in the ingress.
4603///
4604/// This configuration could potentially only lead to an equilibrium when uploading non-full packets
4605/// (ones that can carry at least a single SURB), and the Exit's egress is limiting itself to such a rate.
4606/// If Exit's egress reaches low values due to SURB scarcity, the upper layer protocols over Session might break.
4607///
4608/// #### 4. No SURB balancing on each side
4609///
4610/// 1. The Session initiator (Entry) *DOES* set the [`Capability::NoRateControl`] capability flag when opening Session.
4611/// 2. The Session initiator (Entry) does *NOT* set the [`SurbBalancerConfig`] at all when opening Session.
4612///
4613/// In this situation, no additional SURBs are being produced by the Entry and no Session egress rate-limiting
4614/// takes place at the Exit.
4615///
4616/// This configuration can only lead to an equilibrium when Entry sends non-full packets (ones that carry
4617/// at least a single SURB) and the Exit is consuming the SURBs (Session egress) at a slower or equal rate.
4618/// Such configuration is very fragile, as any disturbances in the SURB flow might lead to a packet drop
4619/// at the Exit's egress.
4620///
4621/// ### SURB decay
4622///
4623/// In a hypothetical scenario of a non-zero packet loss, the Session initiator (Entry) might send a
4624/// certain number of SURBs to the Session recipient (Exit), but only a portion of it is actually delivered.
4625/// The Entry has no way of knowing that and assumes that everything has been delivered.
4626/// A similar problem happens when the Exit uses SURBs to construct return packets, but only a portion
4627/// of those packets is actually delivered to the Entry. At this point, the Entry also subtracts
4628/// fewer SURBs from its SURB estimate at the Exit.
4629///
4630/// In both situations, the Entry thinks there are more SURBs available at the Exit than there really are.
4631///
4632/// To compensate for a potential packet loss, the Entry's estimation of Exit's SURB buffer is regularly
4633/// diminished by a percentage of the `target_surb_buffer_size`, even if no incoming traffic from the
4634/// Exit is detected.
4635///
4636/// This behavior can be controlled via the `surb_decay` field of [`SurbBalancerConfig`].
4637///
4638/// ### SURB balance and target notification
4639///
4640/// The Session recipient (Exit) can notify the Session initiator (Entry) periodically about its estimated
4641/// number of SURBs for the Session. This can help the Entry to adjust its approximation of that level so
4642/// that its Local SURB balancer can better intervene.
4643/// This can be set using the `surb_balance_notify_period` field of [`SessionManagerConfig`] for the Exit.
4644///
4645/// Likewise, the Entry can inform the Exit about its desired SURB buffer target so that the Exit
4646/// can better accommodate its Remote SURB balancing.
4647/// This can be set using the `surb_target_notify` field of the [`SessionManagerConfig`] of each new Session.
4648///
4649/// Both mechanisms leverage the Keep Alive message to report the respective values.
4650///
4651/// ## PIX (Protocol for Incentivization of eXits) Protocol Flow
4652///
4653/// When a Session is opened with the [`Capability::UsePIX`] flag, the following protocol
4654/// runs between the Entry (initiator) and Exit (recipient) to provide on-chain payment
4655/// guarantees for the data relayed through the Session.
4656///
4657/// ### 1. PIX Parameter Negotiation (Session Initiation)
4658///
4659/// During [`SessionManager::new_session`], the Entry encodes its PIX SSA (Session Stealth
4660/// Address) parameters — a [`PixParams`] quadruple of `polys_per_ssa`, `shares_per_poly`,
4661/// `surplus_shares` and the curve `suite` — into the upper 32 bits of the 64-bit options word
4662/// carried in the most significant 64 bits of the `StartSession.additional_data` field, via
4663/// [`PixParams::into_additional_data`]. The first two describe how many polynomials and shares each
4664/// SSA will use; the third is how many extra shares per polynomial the Entry emits to absorb losses. Those three define
4665/// the data quota per SSA, which is `polys × (threshold + surplus) × SESSION_MTU` — the surplus is priced in rather
4666/// than free, since a cycle emits it whether or not any share is lost (see `pix_params_to_quota`).
4667///
4668/// The fourth is not a dimension and does not enter the quota: it names the elliptic curve the
4669/// Entry's build instantiates PIX over, which fixes the width of every curve-sized field later in
4670/// the handshake. It is fixed at build time on both sides and is therefore not negotiated — the Exit
4671/// refuses anything but its own, below.
4672///
4673/// What is announced is built from the installed [`SsaShareGenerator`]'s
4674/// [`SsaGeneratorConfig`](hopr_protocol_pix::SsaGeneratorConfig), never from the caller: the
4675/// generator is what produces the shares that go on the wire, so advertising anything else would
4676/// let the Session proceed while emitting shares the Exit cannot reconstruct. The dimensions are
4677/// therefore not configurable per Session — [`Capability::UsePIX`] is the whole per-Session switch,
4678/// and a node with no PIX toolbox installed refuses the Session. That check runs before the
4679/// initiation challenge slot is reserved, so a node that cannot serve PIX at all cannot have its
4680/// challenge slots exhausted by repeated requests for it.
4681///
4682/// The caller never needs to know the resulting quota in advance: it is computed node-side and
4683/// handed back per SSA in [`AgreedSsaQuota::quota_per_ssa`], which is what sizes the deposit.
4684///
4685/// On the Exit side, `check_pix_params` validates these parameters against:
4686/// - The protocol ranges, which [`PixParams::try_from_additional_data`] enforces as it unpacks.
4687/// - The configured [`IncomingSessionPixConfig::quota_range`] (by default ≈157 MiB–630 MiB). Dynamic admission checks
4688///   the smallest `batch_size × quota_per_ssa` up to the configured maximum; fixed admission checks the per-SSA quota
4689///   itself and retains the configured exact batch.
4690/// - Optionally, [`IncomingSessionPixConfig::enforce_pix`] rejects Sessions that do not offer PIX.
4691/// - The Exit only checks the *product* `polys × (threshold + surplus)`, not the individual values, so the Entry can
4692///   split it to suit its computing power. The computation is easily parallelizable in the number of polynomials, but
4693///   not in threshold. The surplus is inside that product, so redundancy is bought rather than taken: a cycle emits
4694///   `threshold + surplus` shares per polynomial come what may, and the deposit covers all of them.
4695///
4696/// If parameters are rejected, a [`StartErrorReason::UnacceptablePixParams`] error is returned.
4697///
4698/// ### 2. Exit SSA Request (`SsaRequest` → Entry)
4699///
4700/// Once the PIX parameters are accepted, the Exit spawns a `SessionPixSupervisor`, whose opening
4701/// `RequestSsa` action has `send_ssa_request` create a new SSA commitment via the server-side
4702/// [`SsaReconstructor`]. This produces an *Exit commitment* (a group element) that is sent back to
4703/// the Entry as a [`SsaServerCommitmentMessage`].
4704///
4705/// One action, and therefore one message, carries the batch selected during admission: no more than
4706/// [`SupervisorConfig::ssas_per_request`](crate::SupervisorConfig::ssas_per_request) SSAs at
4707/// contiguous indices, sharing the single `params` field, since every SSA in a Session uses the same
4708/// dimensions. The Entry caps what it will accept at
4709/// [`SessionManagerConfig::max_ssas_per_ssa_request`], and rejects an over-cap request in full while
4710/// replying with an `UnacceptablePixParams` [`StartErrorType`], so the Exit does not have to infer the
4711/// refusal from a deadline. The default is a batch of one, which is byte-for-byte the unbatched
4712/// exchange.
4713///
4714/// From here the supervisor owns the cycle's deadlines: `max_ssa_delivery_time` for the Entry's
4715/// commitment, then `max_deposit_wait` for the funds, then the recovery deadlines. Missing any of
4716/// them closes the Session with `ClosureReason::PixFailure`. The first two are multiplied by the batch
4717/// size, because a batch asks the Entry for that many commitment sets and that many deposits before
4718/// any of them can fairly be called late.
4719///
4720/// The opening request is re-sent too, but on its own rule: it has no predecessor, and so a bounded number of
4721/// times (`max_opening_ssa_request_resends`) with gaps that double and never at or after its deadline, which
4722/// it leaves alone, since only a loss on the return path can keep it unanswered. A *successor* request is
4723/// re-sent without a count: the Entry's successor gate drops
4724/// one that comes before its predecessor's returned packets have earned it, and says nothing, and a
